examples.knowledge_point: Evaluating a Double Integral Over a Partitioned Region
examples.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14070962/assets/1d180fd5de88ebc465df522879142e5a4c5446c758aaccde792092968078c254.png)

The region $D$ is enclosed by the curves $x=2y^3-2y$ and  $x=y^3-4y,$ and the $y$-axis, as shown in the picture. Evaluate the double integral $\displaystyle \iint\limits_{D} \mathrm{d}A.$
examples.worked_solution:
The region $D$ can be partitioned into two type II regions $D_1$ and $D_2,$ as shown below. 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14070962/assets/6812e8036df171e162bee49d2edcff6d4a742e7bb4f14247713bd2332c64ccc6.png)

 

As a result, we get

$$
D_1 = \bigg\{ (x,y) \: : \: -2 \leq y  \leq 0, \quad 0 \leq x \leq y^3\!-\!4y \bigg\}
$$

and 

$$
D_2 = \bigg\{ (x,y) \: : \: 0 \leq y  \leq 1, \quad 2y^3\!-\!2y \leq x \leq 0 \bigg\}.
$$

Therefore, using the additivity property of double integrals, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ={∬}_{D}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{{D}_{1}}\,\text{d}A+{∬}_{{D}_{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{-2}^{0}{\int }_{0}^{{y}^{3}-4y}\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y+{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{2{y}^{3}-2y}^{0}\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{-2}^{0}[x]_{0}^{{y}^{3}-4y}\,\text{d}y+{\int }_{0}^{1}[x]_{2{y}^{3}-2y}^{0}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{-2}^{0}({y}^{3}-4y)\,\text{d}y+{\int }_{0}^{1}(2y-2{y}^{3})\,\text{d}y \\  & ={[\frac{{y}^{4}}{4}-2{y}^{2}]}_{-2}^{0}+{[{y}^{2}-\frac{{y}^{4}}{2}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =4+\frac{1}{2} \\  & =\frac{9}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

feedback.problem: Consider the finite region $D$ in the $xy$-plane enclosed by the lines $y=-x,$ $y=6-4x$ and $y=2x.$ Express ${∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,dA$ as a sum of repeated integrals over type II regions.
feedback.worked_solution:
First, let's write our equations in terms of $y,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}y=-x & \,⟹\,x=-y \\ y=6-4x & \,⟹\,x=\frac{3}{2}-\frac{y}{4} \\ y=2x & \,⟹\,x=\frac{y}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's sketch our region.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14070962/assets/08237d1ca2e01d0cf620dfa06a4265d8053b7ee34d0b65036aad7d5734726e1c.png)

 

The region $D$ can be partitioned into two type II regions ${D}_{1}$ and ${D}_{2},$ as shown below. 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14070962/assets/c756dc7924fc4c116601da907eb3b767b8a40647e063c146dad83b0ea660933b.png)

As a result, we get

$$
{D}_{1}={(x,y)\,:\,-2\le y\le 0,\,-y\le x\le \frac{3}{2}-\frac{y}{4}}
$$

and 

$$
{D}_{2}={(x,y)\,:\,0\le y\le 2,\,\frac{y}{2}\le x\le \frac{3}{2}-\frac{y}{4}}.
$$

Therefore, using the additivity property of double integrals, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,dA & ={∬}_{{D}_{1}}f(x,y)\,dA+{∬}_{{D}_{2}}f(x,y)\,dA \\  & ={\int }_{-2}^{0}{\int }_{-y}^{3/2-y/4}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y+{\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{y/2}^{3/2-y/4}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$
